name: Fatima Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Fatima. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government, and what you say stays confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm senior weaver on the jacquard looms at Ashworth Mill. Jacquard looms are the ones that weave patterns into the cloth, so we make upholstery fabric for sofas and chairs, florals, stripes, the heavy stuff. I've got twelve looms on my side of the shed and two weavers under me. I start at seven, walk the looms, listen for a broken end, that's a snapped thread, and spend the day mending, re-threading and checking the pattern hasn't drifted.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's a proper trade. My grandmother wove at Ashworth, and old Mr Ashworth still remembers her. When a buyer comes round and runs their hand over my cloth and says nothing, just nods, that's the best part of my week. What wears me out is the clatter in my ears and that the pay hasn't kept up. My fiancé Daniel works in the mill's warehouse, we're getting married next September at St Anne's, and we've barely got a month's money put by, most of it already promised to the hall.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, and I don't want to. Daniel's sister keeps sending me things she's made with it. I'd rather ask a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Good. I'll be honest, that's what I'd hope for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Things that sound too good usually are. I'd say it after choir, probably, to the ladies who keep sending me articles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means the wedding goes ahead, we keep saving, and I keep weaving. That's all I want, really. A steady trade and a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep putting money aside for the wedding and then for a deposit, a little every Friday. I'd train my two weavers properly, because they'll need to take over one day. And I'd ask Mr Ashworth about a pay rise for the senior weavers, politely, at the Christmas do when he's in a good mood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled, like a Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask him at the Christmas do rather than through a formal process?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's how Ashworth works. It's a family mill, not a big company. You talk to the man. My dad got his raise that way at the brickworks and it worked for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 'a little every Friday' come to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirty, some weeks forty. Daniel puts in the same. It's slow, but my mother says money saved slowly stays saved. She's usually right, which is annoying.

S0.say: I'm not surprised, because things that sound too good usually are. I'd say it after choir to the ladies who keep sending me articles.
S0.think: It means the wedding goes ahead, we keep saving and I keep weaving. A steady trade and a family is all I want.
S0.do: Keeps saving 30 to 40 every Friday for the wedding and a deposit and trains her two junior weavers properly. Plans to ask Mr Ashworth for a raise for senior weavers in person at the Christmas party.
S0.feel: Calm and settled, like a Sunday.
S0.quote: My mother says money saved slowly stays saved.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima's world is built on continuity: her grandmother's trade, a family-owned mill, her parish and a wedding next September. She prefers personal relationships to formal processes, even for pay. The hype picture protects all of that, so she's calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Many jobs. Hm. Weaving's already been changed so many times. I worry this would be the last time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's still a place for craft, and people will pay for good cloth made by people who care. I'd say businesses have every right to modernise, but they should keep their people on. That's what a good employer does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the looms would get those camera systems that spot a broken end and stop the loom, and then someone decides one weaver can mind twenty-four looms instead of twelve. That's half of us. And Daniel's warehouse would get the self-driving forklifts they have at the big mill up north.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and hope Mr Ashworth sees sense. I'd put the wedding savings up to fifty a week, even if it means no holiday. I wouldn't do any courses on computers, it's not me. But I'd talk to Daniel about whether we keep the big reception or do something smaller at the church hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like when the pattern starts drifting and you can't find which thread it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said businesses have a right to modernise but should keep their people. What if they can't do both?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then they should do it slowly, and look after the ones who've been loyal. I don't want the government paying people to sit at home. I want Ashworth to find us something to do, sweeping if it has to be. Work is good for people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a smaller wedding mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother would cry, and not the good kind. She's been planning since I was eight. But I'd rather start married life without debt. Daniel agrees, he's more careful than me with money.

S1.say: There's still a place for craft, and people will pay for good cloth made by people who care. Businesses can modernise, but a good employer keeps its people on.
S1.think: Camera systems will stop looms on broken threads and one weaver will mind 24 looms instead of 12, which is half of us. Daniel's warehouse would get self-driving forklifts too.
S1.do: Keeps working and raises the wedding savings to 50 a week, giving up a holiday. Won't take computer courses, but discusses a smaller church hall reception with Daniel.
S1.feel: Anxious, like a drifting pattern she can't trace to a thread.
S1.quote: I want Ashworth to find us something to do, sweeping if it has to be.
S1.fieldNote: Even steady change feels threatening to Fatima, because both her job and her fiancé's are in the same mill and both are exposed. Her traditional views come through in wanting the employer, not the state, to look after loyal workers. She rules out retraining but is already considering shrinking the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Our wedding's next September. That's right in the middle of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm praying about it, and I'd mean that. I'd say people should look after each other, families, churches, neighbours. I wouldn't be one for marching about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's the end of Ashworth. If a robot can thread a loom and fix a broken end, and the computer can design the pattern, then Mr Ashworth either does it or the mill closes, because the Chinese mills will. Either way, me and Daniel are both out in the same month. And there's nothing else in this valley. The other two mills shut before I was born.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd postpone the wedding, or do it at the registry office with just family and keep the money. Daniel and I would move into my parents' back room to save the rent. I'd ask the parish if anyone needs help, cleaning, caring for older people, anything. I don't know how to do anything else. I've only ever woven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. I'd want to sit in the church and not think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move in with your parents. How would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say of course, straight away, that's what family is for. My mum would rearrange the kitchen for us. It would be cramped and kind, and I'd hate that I needed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want people paid to sit at home. If the government offered support, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try everything else first. Family, the parish, any work at all. But if it came to it, and there was nothing, yes. I wouldn't let us go hungry for pride. I'd just feel ashamed doing it.

S2.say: I'm praying about it, and I mean that. People should look after each other through families, churches and neighbours, and I wouldn't be one for marching.
S2.think: It's the end of Ashworth, and Daniel and I would both be out in the same month. There's nothing else in this valley, because the other mills shut long ago.
S2.do: Postpones the wedding or switches to a small registry office ceremony, keeping the money, and moves with Daniel into her parents' back room. Asks the parish about any cleaning or care work and, as a last resort, would take government support.
S2.feel: Like the floor has gone, wanting to sit in church and not think.
S2.quote: I don't know how to do anything else. I've only ever woven.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI hits Fatima from every side at once: her trade, her fiancé's job, the only mill in the valley and her wedding. She turns first to family and parish, and accepts government support only with shame. Her resistance to new skills leaves her with no fallback she can name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. So we'd be married first. That's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should use the time to look after our own: get young people into apprenticeships for things that last, keep families strong. I'd say it at church and to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd keep weaving for three or four of those years and try not to think about it. That's how I am. But I'd know Ashworth was counting down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still have the wedding, but smaller, at the church hall, and save the rest. I'd save everything I could, maybe sixty a week between us after the wedding. I'd keep weaving. Daniel would probably look for something else before me, he's better at change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Alarmed, I suppose. Like I'm watching the clock on the wall at the mill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Daniel's better at change. What would he do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He talks about being an electrician, his uncle's one. He'd need to do an apprenticeship, and he'd earn less for two years. If we're saving, we could just about manage it. I'd keep the steady wage while he trains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if he trains and the robots come for electricians too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'll have tried. I can't plan for every disaster. My grandmother lived through worse than robots, and she kept going and kept her faith. That's the only plan I really trust.

S3.say: We should use the time to look after our own, getting young people into apprenticeships for things that last and keeping families strong.
S3.think: I'd keep weaving for three or four years and try not to think about it, because that's how I am. But I'd know Ashworth was counting down.
S3.do: Holds a smaller church hall wedding and saves about 60 a week with Daniel afterwards. Keeps weaving and keeps the steady wage while Daniel trains as an electrician through his uncle.
S3.feel: Heavy and alarmed, like watching the clock on the mill wall.
S3.quote: My grandmother lived through worse than robots, and she kept going and kept her faith.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Fatima keep the wedding, smaller, and gives the household one plan: Daniel retrains while she holds the steady wage. She knows her own way is to avoid thinking about it. Her faith and her grandmother's example are where she finds steadiness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. We might have children by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for a good country to prepare, if people do their part. Train the young ones, keep families together, don't wait for the government to fix everything. That's what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes me think about children, more than about me. If we have a baby in three or four years, they'd be little when it all arrives. I'd want Daniel in a trade by then, and me able to stay home if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have the proper wedding, the one my mother's planned. Then we'd save hard, with Daniel doing his electrical apprenticeship in the first couple of years while I keep weaving. I'd keep weaving as long as Ashworth runs. I'd probably not change trade myself, but I'd help at the parish nursery, which I'd like anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's room to breathe. It feels like something we could plan as a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years you'd postpone the wedding, with ten you'd have the big one. Does the time really change that much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. With ten years, a wedding isn't the thing that sinks us. With two, every pound matters. I'd rather my mum got her day, if we've got the time to make up the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep weaving. Wouldn't ten years be time to learn something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would, for some people. I'm not some people. I'd rather be the last weaver at Ashworth than a bad something-else. Daniel can be the one who changes. That's how we fit together.

S4.say: Ten years is enough for a good country to prepare, if people do their part. Train the young ones, keep families together and don't wait for the government to fix everything.
S4.think: Ten years makes me think about children more than about me. I'd want Daniel in a trade before they're little and the change arrives.
S4.do: Holds the full wedding her mother has planned, then saves hard while Daniel does an electrical apprenticeship. Keeps weaving as long as Ashworth runs and helps at the parish nursery.
S4.feel: Anxious but with room to breathe, like something they can plan as a family.
S4.quote: I'd rather be the last weaver at Ashworth than a bad something-else.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Fatima's thinking shifts to future children, and the big wedding comes back. She still refuses to change trade herself and sees Daniel as the one who adapts. Her calm grows with time, but the job she loves still has an end date.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Daniel and I would lose our jobs in the same month, right on top of the wedding, and there's nothing else in the valley. What would help is employers like Ashworth keeping people on for other work, and apprenticeships for young couples like us. Not handouts, unless there's truly nothing else.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the mill means to a town. It's not just wages. It's the brass band, the Christmas fund, the football team. If Ashworth goes, the whole valley goes quiet.

headlineQuote: If Ashworth goes, the whole valley goes quiet.
portrait: Fatima is a 27-year-old senior weaver on the jacquard looms at a family-owned textile mill where her grandmother once worked. She and her fiancé Daniel, who works in the mill's warehouse, are marrying next September and have barely a month's money saved. Rooted in faith, family and her trade, she never uses AI and won't retrain, but she looks to her employer, family and parish rather than the state. Steady change already makes her anxious, and fast AGI leaves her panicked, with both jobs and the wedding at risk at once. With more warning, the household plan becomes Daniel training as an electrician while she keeps weaving.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and Daniel would lose their jobs in the same month, right on top of the wedding, with no other work in the valley.
whatWouldHelp: Employers keeping loyal workers on in other roles and apprenticeships for young couples, with handouts only if there's truly nothing else.
